title: Microsoft Releases TypeScript 7.0 with a Native Go Compiler, Delivering 10x Faster Builds
gist: Microsoft shipped TypeScript 7.0, a faithful rewrite of the TypeScript compiler toolchain in Go, cutting full builds on real codebases by 7.7x-11.9x (VS Code: 125.7s to 10.6s) and editor error-surfacing from ~17.5s to under 1.3s. The release ships without a stable programmatic API, so typescript-eslint, webpack loaders and the Vue/Svelte/Astro/MDX/Angular tooling stack are blocked until 7.1, making the ecosystem's real migration date later than the headline release date.

themes.theme: Go rewrite delivers order-of-magnitude compile speedups

insights.claim: TypeScript 7.0 is the first stable release built on a native compiler ported from TypeScript into Go, and Microsoft states it typically delivers 8x to 12x speedups on full builds.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: A language toolchain crossing an order-of-magnitude perf threshold resets developer-productivity baselines for every enterprise running large TypeScript monorepos.
insights.quote: a faithful port of the toolset from TypeScript into Go that the team says typically delivers speedups of between 8x and 12x on full builds

insights.claim: Microsoft's published benchmarks show full-build times falling from 125.7s to 10.6s on the VS Code source (11.9x), 139.8s to 15.7s on sentry (8.9x), 24.3s to 2.8s on bluesky (8.7x), 12.8s to 1.47s on playwright (8.7x), and 11.2s to 1.46s on tldraw (7.7x).
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: The gains hold across five independent real-world codebases, not a synthetic benchmark, so the speedup is a durable planning assumption rather than marketing.
insights.locator: Microsoft published build times against real codebases

insights.claim: Beyond wall-clock speed, the Go-based TypeScript compiler cut aggregate memory use on the VS Code build by around 18 percent.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Lower memory per type-check job means more parallel CI runners per machine, compounding the compute-cost saving beyond the raw time reduction.
insights.locator: On the VS Code source, a full build fell

insights.claim: TypeScript 7.0 exposes parallelism as tunable configuration via new --checkers and --builders flags, with --singleThreaded available to disable it in constrained environments.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Multi-threading is opt-out, meaning the speedup partly depends on available cores and will under-deliver on small CI containers unless runners are resized.
insights.quote: Parallelism can be tuned with the new --checkers and --builders flags, or switched off entirely with --singleThreaded for constrained environments.
insights.locator: Parallelism can be tuned with the new

themes.theme: Editor latency and CI cost as the real payoff

insights.claim: Because the new TypeScript tooling is built on the Language Server Protocol and uses multiple threads, opening a file with an error in the VS Code codebase dropped from about 17.5 seconds to under 1.3 seconds.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: The LSP rebuild moves TypeScript from batch-tool improvement to interactive-latency improvement, which is where developer-hour savings actually compound.
insights.quote: Editors benefit too, because the new tooling is built on the Language Server Protocol and uses multiple threads.
insights.locator: Editors benefit too, because the new tooling

insights.claim: Slack engineers reported that adopting the native TypeScript compiler cut CI type-checking from about 7.5 minutes to 1.25 minutes.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: A 6x cut in CI type-check time at a company of Slack's scale is a directly quantifiable cloud-compute and engineer-wait-time saving that other large shops can extrapolate.
insights.quote: Slack engineers said the change brought CI type-checking from about 7.5 minutes to 1.25 minutes
insights.locator: Teams testing early releases reported similar gains

insights.claim: Vanta reported high-impact results from adopting tsgo in production, describing the change qualitatively rather than with benchmark figures.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Early enterprise adopters were already running the native compiler before GA, signalling low perceived migration risk among design partners.
insights.quote: Our tsgo adoption at Vanta has been pretty high-impact. Everything is so, so much faster now.
insights.locator: and Vanta reported positive results too

themes.theme: Missing programmatic API gates the ecosystem

insights.claim: TypeScript 7.0 ships without a stable programmatic API, so typescript-eslint and the framework tooling for Vue, Svelte, Astro, MDX and Angular cannot use it until the API lands in 7.1.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: The headline release date is not the ecosystem adoption date; the real inflection for framework and lint tooling is 7.1, one release cycle away.
insights.quote: TypeScript 7.0 ships without a stable programmatic API, which the team expects to land in 7.1
insights.locator: TypeScript 7.0 ships without a stable programmatic API

insights.claim: Projects built on webpack loaders cannot upgrade to the native TypeScript compiler at 7.0 because no API surface exists for loaders to hook into, per a commenter on Microsoft's release blog.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: The large installed base of webpack-based enterprise builds is excluded from day-one adoption, damping the near-term measurable impact of the release.
insights.quote: there seems to be no API surface in the 7.0 release for webpack loaders to utilize.
insights.locator: Elsewhere a commenter on the blog noted

insights.claim: Microsoft has committed to a release cadence of every three to four months for TypeScript now that the Go port has shipped, with 7.1 explicitly scoped to the programmatic API the ecosystem is waiting on.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Puts a roughly Q4 2026 window on full ecosystem unblocking and signals that feature velocity, frozen during the port, resumes now.
insights.quote: with new releases expected every three to four months and 7.1 focused on the API the wider ecosystem is waiting on
insights.locator: The team says feature work resumes now

themes.theme: Migration engineered as a side-by-side path

insights.claim: Microsoft shipped a compatibility package, @typescript/typescript6, that provides a tsc6 binary and re-exports the 6.0 API through npm aliases so existing tooling keeps working alongside the new compiler.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: The dual-binary escape hatch is the mechanism that makes incremental enterprise migration viable and reduces the risk of a stalled upgrade cycle.
insights.quote: Microsoft published a compatibility package, @typescript/typescript6, that provides a tsc6 binary and re-exports the 6.0 API so existing tooling keeps working, wired up through npm aliases.
insights.locator: That side-by-side path is central to migration

insights.claim: TypeScript 7.0 converts 6.0's deprecations into hard errors and makes strict and esnext the defaults, so Microsoft recommends adopting 6.0 first as a staging step.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: The upgrade is a two-hop migration, not one, so realistic enterprise timelines to 7.0 are longer than the perf numbers suggest.
insights.quote: TypeScript 7.0 also turns 6.0's deprecations into hard errors, with strict and esnext now the defaults, so the team recommends adopting TypeScript 6.0 first to smooth the jump.

insights.claim: The native TypeScript port was validated at scale before GA, reaching over 8.5 million weekly downloads as the @typescript/native-preview package after being announced as an experiment in March 2025.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Roughly 17 months of high-volume community preview usage lowers the odds of a post-GA regression wave and supports faster mainstream adoption.
insights.locator: The project began as an experimental native port

themes.theme: Competitive squeeze on type-stripping build tools

insights.claim: TypeScript 7.0 closes much of the speed gap to esbuild, swc and Biome while retaining full type-checking, which those tools omit by stripping or transpiling types without checking them.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: Erodes the core value proposition of the third-party fast-transpiler ecosystem; watch whether esbuild/swc/Biome-adjacent tooling loses mindshare as the speed argument for bypassing tsc weakens.
insights.quote: Unlike faster tools such as esbuild, swc and Biome, which strip or transpile types without checking them, TypeScript 7.0 keeps full type-checking while closing much of the speed gap.
insights.locator: Unlike faster tools such as esbuild, swc and Biome

insights.claim: Microsoft chose Go, not Rust or C++, as the implementation language for a flagship compiler it maintains under the Apache 2.0 license, and returned nightly builds to the standard typescript package on the next tag.
insights.speaker: Daniel Curtis
insights.so_what: A major Microsoft toolchain standardising on Go rather than Rust is a directional signal for systems-language choice in developer-tooling projects.
insights.locator: With 7.0, nightly builds move back under the standard typescript package
